title: Developing a departmental lesson structure – Part 1
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton shares the five-phase departmental lesson structure he built with one maths department, following his argument for centrally planned lessons. The phases are a retrieval Do Now, a prerequisite check, explanation and model, fluency practice and problem solving, each with timings and specific pedagogy such as 80 percent mini-whiteboard thresholds, the 4-2 approach and Turn and Talk. He pre-empts objections about rigidity, and explains why a plenary or exit ticket and atomisation were left out. The piece is a concrete template that other departments can compare against.
points: A rigid starting structure gives teachers something to get better at, with exceptions made deliberately rather than by default.
Separating the unrelated-retrieval Do Now from a snappy prerequisite check preserves routines and timing.
Mini-whiteboard checks with an explicit 80 percent threshold decide whether to move on or explain and re-check, in every phase.
Dropping the plenary frees minutes for daily non-routine problem solving, since constant whiteboard use already gives a reliable read on understanding.
quotes: This is true. But it is a useful unit to start with. Over time, teachers can be encouraged to flex – rolling one lesson over into two, for example, if students need more time to consolidate. But I believe in the benefits of routines and structure, and with everything else in schools dictated to by the bell, I am happy to start thinking about planning in terms of individual lessons that form part of a logical sequence.

Yep, fair point. But such lessons are the exceptions. If we instead start with the assumption that all lessons can be made to fit this structure and only break this when absolutely necessary - perhaps students are going over an assessment or working on a project - then we have a structure that teachers can get better at, and that is ready to be adapted when needed.

This has led to a smoother start to lessons, and mini-whiteboards have bled through to other parts of the lesson, such as the modelling phase and when answers are assessed at the end of independent practice. We also worked on embedding checks for listening throughout the lesson to improve student attention. Colleagues responded well to the call for more consistency and appreciated the extra direction.
As I discuss here, I don’t think it is a good idea to include prerequisite knowledge questions in the Do Now. So, this is a separate phase of the lesson.
As I discuss here, not enough students are exposed to regular opportunities to think about non-routine questions. In this structure, this happens every lesson for all students.

Notice the lack of a plenary or an Exit Ticket. These can be useful for getting a final snapshot of student understanding. However, if mini-whiteboards are used throughout the lesson, as they are in this structure, then the teacher should already have a reliable sense of student understanding. Hence, I would rather allocate those precious minutes to the problem-solving section.

Notice also that there’s no mention of Atomisation. This process fits into this structure but is much more complex to plan and teach effectively. So, we decided to leave it out for now until the other aspects of the lesson structure were secure.
